Module 2

The kernel: system calls, files, memory and programs

Module 1 followed both systems from power-on to the first user program: COMMAND.COM on MS-DOS 4.00, /sbin/init on FreeBSD 15.1. This module studies what runs underneath: the kernel. We look at how a program asks for a service, how open files are represented, how both kernels implement the same FAT file system, how memory is handed out, how programs are loaded and terminated, how drivers are called, and what each kernel does about concurrency. Every claim is tied to a line of the MS-DOS 4.00 source or of FreeBSD 15.1 (release/15.1.0). Module 3 then looks at the shells on top.

MS-DOS 2d04cacFreeBSD release/15.1.040 source listings4 study cases7 exercisesabout 90 min read
Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • explain the difference between a set of services in one shared real-mode address space (MS-DOS) and a protected, privileged kernel with per-process virtual address spaces (FreeBSD);
  • trace a system call from the calling instruction to the handler and back in both systems, naming the stack used at each step and the way errors are reported (the carry flag in both);
  • draw the data structures behind a file handle in both systems (JFT and SFT; descriptor table, struct file and vnode) and predict what dup, dup2 and process creation do to them;
  • decode a FAT12 entry by hand and match the decoding against FAT.ASM and msdosfs_fat.c;
  • walk the MS-DOS memory arena (MCB chain) and read a FreeBSD process memory map (procstat -v);
  • compare MS-DOS EXEC with FreeBSD fork plus execve, including what the child inherits;
  • describe the MS-DOS installable device driver interface and FreeBSD's cdevsw, and explain why both use the word "strategy";
  • explain why MS-DOS is not re-entrant and how TSR programs live with that, and contrast this with the locking discipline of an SMP kernel.

Prerequisites.

  • Module 1 (boot), in particular SYSINIT and CONFIG.SYS on MS-DOS and mi_startup on FreeBSD.
  • The lab environment from Module 0 (00-lab.md): the MS-DOS 4.00 floppy image build/images/dos400.img, tools/dos_run.py to run commands in it, DOSBox-X (or QEMU), and the FreeBSD 15.1 VM with /usr/src.
  • C, and enough x86 assembly to read MOV, PUSH, CALL and INT. Real mode is reviewed below.

2.1 What "kernel" means in each system#

Real mode in brief#

MS-DOS 4.00 runs the processor in real mode, the only mode of the 8086/8088. An address is a 16-bit segment and a 16-bit offset, written segment:offset; the linear address is segment * 16 + offset, so 0000:7C00 and 07C0:0000 both mean linear 0x7C00. That gives 20 bits, 1 MB. A 16-byte unit starting at a multiple of 16 is a paragraph, and a segment value is a paragraph number; MS-DOS measures memory blocks in paragraphs. The segment registers are CS, DS, SS (the stack is SS:SP) and ES. Nothing checks an address: any program can read or write any byte of the 1 MB.

The first 1024 bytes (linear 0x00000-0x003FF) hold the interrupt vector table (IVT): 256 four-byte far pointers. INT n pushes FLAGS, CS and IP, clears the interrupt-enable flag IF and jumps through the pointer at 0000:(4*n); IRET pops the three words. A software interrupt is thus an indirect far call through a table that every program can rewrite. MS-DOS uses vectors 20h-2Ah (VECTOR.INC lines 6-33): 20h terminate, 21h the system call, 22h-24h the terminate, Ctrl-C and critical-error (hard error) handlers, 25h/26h absolute disk read/write, 27h terminate-and-stay-resident, 28h the idle call and 2Ah critical sections.

MS-DOS 4.00: a library behind INT 21h#

The resident system is two files: IO.SYS, built from v4.0/src/BIOS with the built-in device drivers (BIOS/MAKEFILE lines 3-13), and MSDOS.SYS, linked from the objects in DOS/MSDOS.LNK (DOS/MAKEFILE lines 208-220). This module is about MSDOS.SYS. A note on the tree: DOS/DISPATCH.ASM ("Created: MZ 30 March 1983", DISPATCH.ASM lines 4-8) is not part of the build: nothing includes it and the link list does not name it. The assembled dispatcher is DISP.ASM, included by MSDISP.ASM (MSDISP.ASM lines 7-15); likewise MS_TABLE.ASM is assembled through INC/MSTABLE.ASM and MS_CODE.ASM through MSCODE.ASM.

After boot, MSDOS.SYS behaves like a library shared by every program: one address space, one copy of every DOS variable, no privilege levels, no memory protection. DOS does not even own its entry point. Functions 25h and 35h set and get vectors, but they are plain stores and loads (Listing 2.1).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.1 – Setting an interrupt vector is a plain store into the IVT at segment 0 (GETSET.ASM lines 682-744)Source ↗
        procedure   $SET_INTERRUPT_VECTOR,NEAR
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING

; Inputs:
;       AL = interrupt number
;       DS:DX is desired new interrupt vector
; Function:
;       Set the interrupt vector
; Returns:
;       None

        CALL    RECSET
        CLI                             ; Watch out!!!!! Folks sometimes use
        MOV     ES:[BX],DX              ;   this for hardware ints (like timer).
        MOV     ES:[BX+2],DS
        STI
        return
EndProc $SET_INTERRUPT_VECTOR
⋮
procedure   RECSET,NEAR
⋮
        XOR     BX,BX
        MOV     ES,BX
        MOV     BL,AL
        SHL     BX,1
        SHL     BX,1
        return
EndProc recset

RECSET points ES:BX at IVT entry AL. The CLI/STI pair is the only safeguard, and its comment says why: programs hook hardware interrupts such as the timer this way. A program may also write 0000:0084 (the INT 21h vector) directly. Resident utilities (TSRs, Section 2.2.4) and network redirectors depend on this freedom, a reasonable design for a one-user 8088 with 256-640 KB of RAM and no memory-management hardware.

FreeBSD 15.1: a privileged kernel#

FreeBSD runs the amd64 processor in 64-bit long mode with paging. The kernel executes at privilege level 0; user programs execute at level 3 and can neither execute privileged instructions nor reach memory that their page tables do not map. Every process has its own virtual address space, described by a struct vm_map (Section 2.5). The kernel half of the address space is the same in every process and is protected from user mode (with the page-table isolation mitigation enabled, most of it is not even mapped while user code runs; this is why there is a fast_syscall_pti entry next to the one in Listing 2.11). The only ways into the kernel are system calls, processor exceptions (for example page faults) and hardware interrupts, and the entry points are set by the kernel alone. Interrupt handlers are registered by kernel code; a user process that wants to react to events uses signals, which the kernel delivers.

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1 (amd64)
CPU mode real mode, 16-bit long mode, 64-bit, paging
Privilege separation none kernel ring 0, user ring 3
Address spaces one, 1 MB, shared by DOS and all programs one per process, plus the kernel
Who may change interrupt vectors any program only the kernel
Programs running at once one (plus TSRs that borrow the CPU) many processes, many threads, many CPUs
Kernel written in 8086 assembly (MASM) C, with a little assembly

The left side is schematic: the ROM BIOS keeps its data at segment 40h (BIOSEG, MSHARD.ASM line 20), SYSINIT (Module 1) decides where the DOS tables go, and some of them end up as blocks inside the arena. The right side is described exactly by the vm_map of each process, which you will print with procstat -v in Study case 2.C.

2.2 Entering the kernel: INT 21h and the syscall instruction#

2.2.1 The INT 21h calling convention#

An MS-DOS system call puts a function number in AH, arguments in other registers, and executes INT 21h. Pointers are segment:offset pairs, usually DS:DX. The handle, directory, memory and process calls (39h and up) return with the carry flag clear on success, or set with an error code in AX. The source documents each call in a comment block, for example read in HANDLE.ASM lines 328-341.

Example 2.1 – Reading 512 bytes from an open handle (illustrative code, not from the tree)
        mov     ah, 3Fh         ; function 3Fh: read from file or device
        mov     bx, [handle]    ; handle returned by function 3Dh (open)
        mov     cx, 512         ; byte count
        mov     dx, buffer      ; DS:DX -> caller's buffer
        int     21h
        jc      read_failed     ; CF=1: AX = error code (6 = invalid handle)
        ; CF=0: AX = number of bytes actually read

2.2.2 The dispatcher#

The INT 21h vector points at the label COMMAND in DISP.ASM (Listing 2.2). INT has already pushed FLAGS, CS and IP on the caller's stack and cleared IF, so interrupts are off.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.2 – The INT 21h entry point: range check, interrupt-off fast path, register save (DISP.ASM lines 228-271)Source ↗
entry   COMMAND                         ; Interrupt call entry point (INT 21H)
⋮
        CMP     AH,MAXCOM
        JA      BadCall
⋮
SAVREGS:
        CMP     AH,GET_CURRENT_PDB
        JZ      $GET_CURRENT_PDB
        CMP     AH,GetCurrentPSP
        JZ      $GET_CURRENT_PDB
        CMP     AH,SET_CURRENT_PDB
        JZ      $SET_CURRENT_PDB
        CMP     AH,Set_CTRL_C_Trapping
        JNZ     chkprt
        JMP     $Set_CTRL_C_Trapping
chkprt:
        CMP     AH,SET_PRINTER_FLAG
        JZ      $Set_Printer_Flag
⋮
; Preserve all user's registers on his own stack.
;
        CALL    save_world
        MOV     [SaveDS],DS
        MOV     [SaveBX],BX
        MOV     BX,CS
        MOV     DS,BX
        ASSUME  DS:DOSGROUP
        INC     [INDOS]                 ; Flag that we're in the DOS
        XOR     AX,AX
        MOV     [USER_ID],AX
        MOV     AX,CurrentPDB           ; current process
        MOV     [PROC_ID],AX            ; Assume local machine for the moment

What to notice:

  • A function number above MAXCOM (the last table index, 6Ch in MS-DOS 4.00, MS_TABLE.ASM lines 234-237 and MS_TABLE.ASM lines 405-409) goes to BADCALL, which returns AL=0 without setting carry, because that "may break some programs" (DISP.ASM lines 192-200).
  • Five calls (get/set current PSP, Ctrl-C state, printer flag) are answered at once, on the caller's stack with interrupts off, because a network server issues them "at arbitrary times" (DISP.ASM lines 240-243).
  • save_world (DISP.ASM lines 444-456) pushes ES DS BP DI SI DX CX BX AX on the caller's stack. With the three words pushed by INT this forms the user register frame, user_environ (DOSSYM.INC lines 58-71). The handlers still receive the caller's registers directly (the dispatcher restores BX and DS just before the call), and they write results into the frame via get_user_stack (DISP.ASM lines 545-548).
  • INC [INDOS] marks "a DOS call is in progress": the InDOS flag.

The dispatcher then leaves the caller's stack (Listing 2.3).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.3 – Saving the caller's SS:SP and switching to a DOS stack (DISP.ASM lines 273-299)Source ↗
; Provide one level of reentrancy for INT 24 recallability.
;
        MOV     AX,[user_SP]
        MOV     [NSP],AX
        MOV     AX,[user_SS]
        MOV     [NSS],AX
        POP     AX
        PUSH    AX
        MOV     [user_SP],SP
        MOV     [user_SS],SS
;
; save user stack in his area for later returns (possibly from EXEC)
;
        MOV     DS,[CurrentPDB]
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[PDB_User_stack],SP
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[PDB_User_stack+2],SS

        MOV     fSharing,0              ; allow redirection

        MOV     BX,CS                   ; no holes here.
        MOV     SS,BX
ASSUME  SS:DOSGROUP

entry   REDISP
        MOV     SP,OFFSET DOSGROUP:AUXSTACK ; Enough stack for interrupts
        STI                             ; stack is in our space now...

The caller's SS:SP, which now points at the register frame, is saved in the globals User_SS:User_SP and in the PDB_User_stack field of the current program's Program Segment Prefix (PSP, the 256-byte header in front of every program, Section 2.3). The previous pair goes to NSS:NSP, "one level of reentrancy for INT 24". Then SS becomes the DOS segment (DOSGROUP), SP the top of AUXSTACK, and only then are interrupts enabled.

MS-DOS has three internal stacks of StackSize = 180h (384) bytes, AUXSTACK, DSKSTACK and IOSTACK (MS_DATA.ASM lines 138-157). The dispatcher picks one per call (Listing 2.4).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.4 – Choosing a stack and calling through the dispatch table (DISP.ASM lines 331-399)Source ↗
        OR      AH,AH
        JZ      DSKROUT                 ; ABORT
⋮
        CMP     AH,GetExtendedError
        JZ      DISPCALL
⋮
        CMP     AH,12
        JA      DSKROUT
        CMP     [ERRORMODE],0           ; Are we in an INT 24?
        JNZ     DISPCALL                ; Stay on AUXSTACK if INT 24.
        MOV     SP,OFFSET DOSGROUP:IOSTACK
        JMP     SHORT DISPCALL
⋮
DSKROUT:
        MOV     [USER_IN_AX],AX         ; Remember what user is doing
        MOV     [EXTERR_LOCUS],errLOC_Unk ; Default
        MOV     [ERRORMODE],0           ; Cannot make non 1-12 calls in
        MOV     [WPERR],-1              ; error mode, so good place to make
⋮
        MOV     IdleInt,0
        MOV     SP,OFFSET DOSGROUP:DSKSTACK
        TEST    [CNTCFLAG],-1
        JZ      DISPCALL                ; Extra ^C checking is disabled
        PUSH    AX
        invoke  DSKSTATCHK
        POP     AX
DISPCALL:
        MOV     BX,CS:Dispatch[BX]
        XCHG    BX,SaveBX
        MOV     DS,SaveDS
⋮
        ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        CALL    SaveBX
Stack Used for Why
AUXSTACK briefly by every call; throughout for 59h and for calls 01h-0Ch made inside an INT 24h handler must work while a critical-error handler is active
IOSTACK calls 01h-0Ch (CP/M-style character I/O) they may wait for a key and issue INT 28h
DSKSTACK everything else, including 00h (terminate) disk and file calls, which may raise INT 24h

The dispatch itself is MOV BX,CS:Dispatch[BX], a 16-bit near address from a table indexed by AH*2, and CALL SaveBX. Listing 2.5 shows part of the table.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.5 – Part of the INT 21h dispatch table (AH = 3Ch-4Fh) (MS_TABLE.ASM lines 334-357)Source ↗
;   File Group
        short_addr  $CREAT                          ; 60     3C
        short_addr  $OPEN                           ; 61     3D
        short_addr  $CLOSE                          ; 62     3E
        short_addr  $READ                           ; 63     3F
        short_addr  $WRITE                          ; 64     40
        short_addr  $UNLINK                         ; 65     41
        short_addr  $LSEEK                          ; 66     42
        short_addr  $CHMOD                          ; 67     43
        short_addr  $IOCTL                          ; 68     44
        short_addr  $DUP                            ; 69     45
        short_addr  $DUP2                           ; 70     46
        short_addr  $CURRENT_DIR                    ; 71     47
;    Memory Group
        short_addr  $ALLOC                          ; 72     48
        short_addr  $DEALLOC                        ; 73     49
        short_addr  $SETBLOCK                       ; 74     4A
;    Process Group
        short_addr  $EXEC                           ; 75     4B
        short_addr  $EXIT                           ; 76     4C
        short_addr  $WAIT                           ; 77     4D
        short_addr  $FIND_FIRST                     ; 78     4E
;   Special Group
        short_addr  $FIND_NEXT                      ; 79     4F

The source labels this group XENIX CALLS (MS_TABLE.ASM lines 329-336): the handle, directory, memory and process calls added for MS-DOS 2.x (ALLOC.ASM lines 5-6) follow the Unix model (XENIX was Microsoft's Unix). That is why open/read/dup/exec can be compared across the two systems almost name for name.

2.2.3 Returning and reporting errors#

Handle-style calls end by jumping to SYS_RET_OK or SYS_RET_ERR (Listing 2.6), which clear or set the carry bit in the saved flags word of the caller's frame and store AX there. IRET reloads FLAGS from the frame, so the caller sees CF as written.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.6 – Success and error returns: the carry bit is set in the caller's saved flags (MS_CODE.ASM lines 292-310)Source ↗
procedure   SYS_RETURN,NEAR
        ASSUME  DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING
entry   SYS_RET_OK
        invoke  FETCHI_CHECK            ; TAG checking for FETCHI
        invoke  get_user_stack
        AND     [SI.user_F],NOT f_Carry ; turn off user's carry flag
        JMP     SHORT DO_RET            ; carry is now clear

entry   SYS_RET_ERR
        XOR     AH,AH                   ; hack to allow for smaller error rets
        invoke  ETAB_LK                 ; Make sure code is OK, EXTERR gets set
        CALL    ErrorMap
entry   From_GetSet
        invoke  get_user_stack
        OR      [SI.user_F],f_Carry     ; signal carry to user
        STC                             ; also, signal internal error
DO_RET:
        MOV     [SI.user_AX],AX         ; Really only sets AH
        return

ETAB_LK and ErrorMap record the real error for function 59h (Get Extended Error) and, if needed, substitute a code the call was documented to return in older versions, from the per-call list I21_MAP_E_TAB (MS_TABLE.ASM lines 32-62). Read, for instance, may only return 6 (invalid handle) or 5 (access denied) (MS_TABLE.ASM line 78). Finally LEAVEDOS (DISP.ASM lines 405-418) disables interrupts, decrements InDOS, reloads the caller's SS:SP, stores AL into the frame (the CP/M-style calls return only AL), restores NSS:NSP, pops the registers and executes IRET.

2.2.4 InDOS, the critical-error flag, and why MS-DOS is not re-entrant#

A routine is re-entrant if it can be entered again, for example from an interrupt handler, before an earlier activation finishes, without corrupting either. MS-DOS is not: the caller's stack pointer lives in one global pair with one spare for INT 24h; the three stacks are at fixed addresses, so a second disk call would overwrite the first one's return addresses on DSKSTACK; and dozens of globals (current SFT, current DPB, transfer address, path buffers) describe the call in progress.

A program that may call DOS from an interrupt handler must therefore test two adjacent flags (Listing 2.7). Function 34h returns the address of INDOS in ES:BX (MISC.ASM lines 131-138). ErrorMode, the critical-error flag, is non-zero while the INT 24h handler runs; the source requires it to be the byte before INDOS, at ES:BX-1.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.7 – InDOS and the critical-error flag open the "swappable" data area (CONST2.ASM lines 95-106)Source ↗
;
; WARNING!!!  PRINT and PSPRINT *REQUIRE* ErrorMode to precede INDOS.
; Also, IBM server 1.0 requires this also.
;
        EVEN                    ; Force swap area to start on word boundry
PUBLIC  SWAP_START
SWAP_START      LABEL BYTE
        I_am    ErrorMode,BYTE          ; Flag for INT 24 processing
        I_am    INDOS,BYTE,<0>          ; DOS status for interrupt processing
        I_am    WPErr,BYTE,<-1>         ; Write protect error flag
        I_am    EXTERR_LOCUS,BYTE       ; Extended Error Locus
        I_am    EXTERR,WORD,<0>         ; Extended Error code

The per-call state lies between SWAP_START and SWAP_END (MS_DATA.ASM lines 179-180); function 5D06h returns its address and size (SRVCALL.ASM lines 96-99), so a network server or task switcher can save and restore it and keep several DOS calls in progress with one copy of DOS: the closest MS-DOS comes to a per-thread kernel context.

A TSR (terminate and stay resident program, Section 2.6) that calls DOS from a hotkey or timer interrupt must wait until both flags are 0. That alone would starve it at the C> prompt, where COMMAND.COM sits inside function 0Ah (buffered input, TCODE.ASM lines 359-361) with InDOS = 1. Hence INT 28h, the idle interrupt: while a console call waits for a key, DOS keeps calling SPOOLINT (CPMIO.ASM lines 283-305 shows the polling loop of function 07h).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.8 – SPOOLINT: INT 28h is issued only for calls 01h-0Ch and never during INT 24h (CTRLC.ASM lines 168-189)Source ↗
;
; SpoolInt - signal processes that the DOS is truly idle.  We are allowed to
; do this ONLY if we are working on a 1-12 system call AND if we are not in
; the middle of an INT 24.
;
procedure   SPOOLINT,NEAR
        PUSHF
        test    IdleInt,-1
        jz      POPFRet
        test    ErrorMode,-1
        jnz     POPFRet
;
; Note that we are going to allow an external program to issue system calls
; at this time.  We MUST preserve IdleInt across this.
;
        PUSH    WORD PTR IdleInt
        INT     int_spooler
        POP     WORD PTR IdleInt
POPFRET:
        POPF
        return
EndProc SPOOLINT

IdleInt is set at entry (DISP.ASM line 317) and cleared for every call that runs on DSKSTACK (DISP.ASM lines 372-376). So when INT 28h fires, the interrupted call is on IOSTACK, and the handler may issue calls above 0Ch, which use DSKSTACK. The dispatcher's own comments name PRINT as a program that calls DOS "at INT 28 … time" (DISP.ASM lines 334-336). Exercise 2.5 applies these rules.

2.2.5 FreeBSD: from read() to sys_read()#

A C program calls read(fd, buf, n). In FreeBSD 15 the stubs live in libsys; read is interposed (a threading library may wrap it), so libc's read calls through a table (read.c lines 37-42) whose slot points at __sys_read (interposing_table.c line 51). Each stub is a generated one-line assembly file (Makefile.sys lines 151-164) expanding the macros of Listing 2.9.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.9 – The amd64 system call stub: number in %eax, then syscall, then "jb cerror" (SYS.h lines 38-59)Source ↗
#define _SYSCALL(name)                                                  \
                        mov $SYS_##name, %eax;                          \
                        movq %rcx, %r10;                                \
                        syscall

#ifndef _SYSCALL_BODY
#define _SYSCALL_BODY(name)                                             \
                        _SYSCALL(name);                                 \
                        jb HIDENAME(cerror);                            \
                        ret
#endif

#define RSYSCALL(name)  ENTRY(__sys_##name);                            \
                        WEAK_REFERENCE(__sys_##name, name);             \
                        WEAK_REFERENCE(__sys_##name, _##name);          \
                        _SYSCALL_BODY(name);                            \
                        END(__sys_##name)

#define PSEUDO(name)    ENTRY(__sys_##name);                            \
                        WEAK_REFERENCE(__sys_##name, _##name);          \
                        _SYSCALL_BODY(name);                            \
                        END(__sys_##name)

_SYSCALL puts the call number in %eax, copies the fourth argument from %rcx to %r10 (the syscall instruction overwrites %rcx with the return address and %r11 with RFLAGS) and executes syscall. Arguments travel in %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %r10, %r8, %r9. Afterwards jb ("jump if below") jumps if the carry flag is set, to cerror (Listing 2.10), which stores the error number in errno and returns -1: the same user-side convention as MS-DOS, hidden behind errno.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.10 – cerror: error code from %rax into errno, return -1 (cerror.S lines 46-53)Source ↗
HIDENAME(cerror):
        pushq   %rax
        call    PIC_PLT(CNAME(__error))
        popq    %rcx
        movl    %ecx,(%rax)
        movq    $-1,%rax
        movq    $-1,%rdx
        ret

syscall switches to ring 0 and jumps to the address the kernel wrote into the MSR_LSTAR register (machdep.c lines 1189-1190): fast_syscall (Listing 2.11). The instruction does not switch stacks, so the first job is to find the current thread's kernel stack.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.11 – fast_syscall: switch to the kernel stack, build a trap frame, call amd64_syscall (exception.S lines 525-570)Source ↗
IDTVEC(fast_syscall)
        swapgs
fast_syscall_common:
        movq    %rsp,PCPU(SCRATCH_RSP)
        movq    PCPU(RSP0),%rsp
        /* Now emulate a trapframe. Make the 8 byte alignment odd for call. */
        subq    $TF_SIZE,%rsp
        /* defer TF_RSP till we have a spare register */
        movq    %r11,TF_RFLAGS(%rsp)
        movq    %rcx,TF_RIP(%rsp)       /* %rcx original value is in %r10 */
        movq    PCPU(SCRATCH_RSP),%r11  /* %r11 already saved */
        movq    %r11,TF_RSP(%rsp)       /* user stack pointer */
⋮
        movq    %rax,TF_RAX(%rsp)       /* syscall number */
        movq    %rdx,TF_RDX(%rsp)       /* arg 3 */
        movq    %r10,TF_RCX(%rsp)       /* arg 4 */
⋮
        sti
⋮
        movq    %rdi,TF_RDI(%rsp)       /* arg 1 */
        movq    %rsi,TF_RSI(%rsp)       /* arg 2 */
        movq    %r8,TF_R8(%rsp)         /* arg 5 */
        movq    %r9,TF_R9(%rsp)         /* arg 6 */
⋮
        movq    PCPU(CURTHREAD),%rdi
        movq    %rsp,TD_FRAME(%rdi)
        movl    TF_RFLAGS(%rsp),%esi
        andl    $PSL_T,%esi
        call    amd64_syscall

swapgs makes %gs point at this CPU's private data (PCPU). The user %rsp is parked in a per-CPU slot, %rsp is loaded with PCPU(RSP0), the top of the current thread's kernel stack, and a struct trapframe is filled with the user registers; sti follows once the frame is safe. This is Listing 2.3 again, with one decisive difference: the kernel stack is per thread, so thousands of system calls can be in progress at once, while MS-DOS has one set of stacks for the whole machine.

amd64_syscall (trap.c lines 1257-1307) calls the machine-independent syscallenter() (subr_syscall.c lines 52-214), which fetches the arguments, calls (se->sy_call)(td, sa->args) (subr_syscall.c lines 192-199) and finally sv_set_syscall_retval (subr_syscall.c line 211). cpu_fetch_syscall_args takes the number from tf_rax, looks it up in p_sysent->sv_table and copies the six register arguments from the trap frame (trap.c lines 1132-1164).

sv_table is the sysent table, an array of struct sysent (sysent.h lines 65-75) with the handler and argument count of each call. It is generated from syscalls.master; Listing 2.12 is the entry for read, number 3, and init_sysent.c line 72 is the generated line pointing at sys_read.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.12 – The read entry in syscalls.master (syscalls.master lines 136-142)Source ↗
3       AUE_READ        STD|CAPENABLED {
                ssize_t read(
                    int fd,
                    _Out_writes_bytes_(nbyte) void *buf,
                    size_t nbyte
                );
        }

A note on copyin. The pointer buf is a user address, and the kernel never dereferences it directly. sys_read describes it in a struct uio marked UIO_USERSPACE (sys_generic.c lines 191-208); the data is moved at the end of the chain by uiomove, which uses copyout (Study case 2.A). String arguments, as in execve, are fetched with copyinstr (kern_exec.c lines 1569-1583). These routines turn a bad user address into EFAULT instead of a crash. MS-DOS just uses the caller's DS:DX, normalised into the global transfer address DMAADD (Align_Buffer, HANDLE.ASM lines 431-445): there is nothing to check, because no address is forbidden.

The result is written back by cpu_set_syscall_retval (Listing 2.13).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.13 – Writing the result: clear PSL_C on success, set it and put the errno value in %rax on failure (vm_machdep.c lines 544-584)Source ↗
void
cpu_set_syscall_retval(struct thread *td, int error)
{
        struct trapframe *frame;

        frame = td->td_frame;
        if (__predict_true(error == 0)) {
                frame->tf_rax = td->td_retval[0];
                frame->tf_rdx = td->td_retval[1];
                frame->tf_rflags &= ~PSL_C;
                return;
        }
⋮
        switch (error) {
        case ERESTART:
⋮
                frame->tf_rip -= frame->tf_err;
                frame->tf_r10 = frame->tf_rcx;
                set_pcb_flags(td->td_pcb, PCB_FULL_IRET);
                break;
⋮
        default:
                frame->tf_rax = error;
                frame->tf_rflags |= PSL_C;
                break;
        }
}

PSL_C is the carry bit of RFLAGS. This is SYS_RET_OK/SYS_RET_ERR from Listing 2.6 again, implemented the same way: by editing the caller's saved flags. ERESTART rewinds %rip by tf_err, which fast_syscall set to 2, the length of syscall (exception.S line 554), so an interrupted call is transparently re-executed. The exit path restores the user registers and executes sysretq (exception.S lines 582-600).

Step MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1 amd64
Instruction INT 21h syscall
Function number AH %eax (SYS_read = 3)
Arguments registers; pointers as DS:DX etc. %rdi %rsi %rdx %r10 %r8 %r9
Entry point set by IVT entry 21h (writable by anyone) MSR written by the kernel
Caller state saved on the caller's stack (save_world) struct trapframe on the thread's kernel stack
Kernel stack one of 3 global 384-byte stacks per-thread kernel stack
Table DISPATCH, 16-bit near pointers sysent[], generated from syscalls.master
Success CF=0, result in AX CF=0, result in %rax (and %rdx)
Failure CF=1, AX = DOS error code CF=1, %rax = errno value; libc sets errno, returns -1
Concurrent calls one at a time (InDOS) many, one per thread

2.3 Files and handles#

MS-DOS: PSP, Job File Table and System File Table#

Every MS-DOS program starts with a Program Segment Prefix (PSP), the process data block (PDB) of the source (Listing 2.14). PDB_JFN_Table is the Job File Table (JFT): 20 bytes (FilPerProc), one per handle, each holding 0FFh (unused) or a System File Number (SFN), an index into the global System File Table (SFT). A handle is just an index into the JFT. By the field sizes, the JFT is at PSP offset 18h, the environment segment at 2Ch, and PDB_JFN_Length/PDB_JFN_Pointer at 32h/34h; these let a program move and enlarge its JFT (function 67h, HANDLE.ASM lines 205-326).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.14 – The PSP ("process data block"): JFT, environment, saved user stack (PDB.INC lines 8-34)Source ↗
FilPerProc          EQU     20
⋮
Process_data_block  STRUC
PDB_Exit_Call       DW      ?           ; INT int_abort system terminate
PDB_block_len       DW      ?           ; size of execution block
                    DB      ?
PDB_CPM_Call        DB  5 DUP (?)       ; ancient call to system
PDB_Exit            DD      ?           ; pointer to exit routine
PDB_Ctrl_C          DD      ?           ; pointer to ^C routine
PDB_Fatal_abort     DD      ?           ; pointer to fatal error
⋮
PDB_Parent_PID      DW      ?           ; PID of parent (terminate PID)
PDB_JFN_Table       DB  FilPerProc DUP (?)
⋮
PDB_environ         DW      ?           ; seg addr of environment
⋮
PDB_User_stack      DD      ?           ; stack of self during system calls
PDB_JFN_Length      DW      ?           ; number of handles allowed
PDB_JFN_Pointer     DD      ?           ; pointer to JFN table
PDB_Next_PDB        DD      ?           ; pointer to nested PDB's

An SFT entry describes one open file: mode, reference count, device or drive, first cluster, size and current position (Listing 2.15); the fields add up to 3Bh (59) bytes. MSDOS.SYS has a built-in table of sf_default_number = 5 entries (CONST2.ASM lines 51-56). FILES= (8 to 255, SYSCONF.ASM lines 395-399; default 8, SYSINIT1.ASM line 272) makes SYSINIT chain a second table of FILES - 5 entries behind it (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 982-1001). When all are in use, every program's open fails with error 4, "too many open files".

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.15 – The System File Table entry (abridged) (SF.INC lines 25-84)Source ↗
sf_entry        STRUC
sf_ref_count    DW      ?               ; number of processes sharing entry
                                        ;   if FCB then ref count
sf_mode         DW      ?               ; mode of access or high bit on if FCB
sf_attr         DB      ?               ; attribute of file
sf_flags        DW      ?               ;Bits 8-15
⋮

⋮

sf_time         DW      ?               ; Time associated with file

sf_size         DD      ?               ; Size associated with file
sf_position     DD      ?               ; Read/Write pointer or LRU count for FCBs

                                        ; for this file
sf_dirpos       DB      ?               ; Offset of this entry in the above
⋮
sf_name         DB      11 DUP (?)      ; 11 character name that is in the
