pJFNFromHandle checks the handle against PDB_JFN_Length and returns a pointer to the JFT byte (UTIL.ASM lines 59-74); Listing 2.16 does the rest. The diagram after it shows example values.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.16 – JFT byte -> SFN -> SFT entry, walking the chain of SFT tables (UTIL.ASM lines 90-137)Source ↗
procedure   SFFromHandle,NEAR
        ASSUME  CS:DOSGROUP,DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING,SS:NOTHING
        CALL    pJFNFromHandle          ; get jfn pointer
        retc                            ; return if error
        CMP     BYTE PTR ES:[DI],-1     ; unused handle
⋮
GetSF:
        SaveReg <BX>                    ; save handle
        MOV     BL,BYTE PTR ES:[DI]     ; get SFN
        XOR     BH,BH                   ; ignore upper half
        CALL    SFFromSFN               ; get real sf spot
⋮
procedure   SFFromSFN,NEAR
        ASSUME  CS:DOSGROUP,DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING,SS:NOTHING
        LES     DI,[SFT_Addr]           ; get pointer to beginning of table
ScanLoop:
        CMP     BX,ES:[DI].SFCount      ; is handle in this table?
        JB      GetOffset               ; yes, go grab it
        SUB     BX,ES:[DI].SFCount
        LES     DI,ES:[DI].SFLink       ; get next table segment
        CMP     DI,-1                   ; end of tables?
⋮
GetOffset:
        SaveReg <AX>                    ; save AX
        MOV     AX,SIZE SF_Entry        ; put it in a nice place
        MUL     BL                      ; times size
        ADD     DI,AX                   ; offset by size
        RestoreReg  <AX>                ; get world back
        ADD     DI,SFTable              ; offset into structure
Diagram
 PSP (per program)            System File Table (global, FILES= entries)
 +---------------+            +-----------------------------------+
 | JFT[0] = 01h -+--.         | SFN 0: AUX ...                    |
 | JFT[1] = 01h -+--+-------> | SFN 1: CON  ref_count=3 -> device |
 | JFT[2] = 01h -+--'         | ...                               |
 | JFT[5] = 07h -+----------> | SFN 7: A:LETTER.TXT ref_count=1   |
 | JFT[6] = 0FFh |  (free)    |        -> DPB of A:, position     |
 +---------------+            +-----------------------------------+

Function 45h (DUP, HANDLE.ASM lines 709-727) finds a free JFT slot with JFNFree, copies the SFN into it, and DOS_Dup_Direct increments sf_ref_count (DUP.ASM lines 50-63). Function 46h (FORCEDUP, $Dup2) closes the target handle and then jumps into the same code (HANDLE.ASM lines 739-747). Both handles now share one SFT entry, hence one file position.

EXEC gives the child a copy of the parent's JFT and increments the reference count of every inherited SFT entry, except entries flagged "no inherit" (sf_no_inherit, SF.INC line 110); Study case 2.D shows the loop. Module 3 shows how COMMAND.COM builds on this inheritance for redirection.

FreeBSD: descriptor table, struct file, vnode#

FreeBSD has the same three levels. Each process has a struct filedesc whose table fd_files is an array of struct filedescent indexed by descriptor number (Listing 2.17). Each entry points to a struct file (file.h lines 200-226), the system-wide open file with reference count f_count, offset f_offset and an operations vector f_ops. For a regular file, f_vnode points to the vnode, the in-memory object for the file itself, shared by all opens of that file.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.17 – Per-process descriptor table (filedesc.h lines 56-124)Source ↗
struct filedescent {
        struct file     *fde_file;      /* file structure for open file */
        struct filecaps  fde_caps;      /* per-descriptor rights */
        uint8_t          fde_flags;     /* per-process open file flags */
        seqc_t           fde_seqc;      /* keep file and caps in sync */
};
⋮
struct fdescenttbl {
        int     fdt_nfiles;             /* number of open files allocated */
        struct  filedescent fdt_ofiles[0];      /* open files */
};
⋮
struct filedesc {
        struct  fdescenttbl *fd_files;  /* open files table */
        NDSLOTTYPE *fd_map;             /* bitmap of free fds */
        int     fd_freefile;            /* approx. next free file */
        int     fd_refcnt;              /* thread reference count */
        int     fd_holdcnt;             /* hold count on structure + mutex */
        struct  sx fd_sx;               /* protects members of this struct */
        struct  kqlist fd_kqlist;       /* list of kqueues on this filedesc */
        int     fd_holdleaderscount;    /* block fdfree() for shared close() */
        int     fd_holdleaderswakeup;   /* fdfree() needs wakeup */
};

A historical detail connects the two systems: the initial FreeBSD table has NDFILE = 20 slots, "selected based the historical limit of 20 open files" (kern_descrip.c lines 132-147), the same 20 as FilPerProc. Unlike the MS-DOS JFT, the FreeBSD table grows on demand up to the RLIMIT_NOFILE resource limit, and there is no fixed FILES= pool: struct file objects are allocated as needed.

dup and dup2 both end in kern_dup (kern_descrip.c lines 374-395). Listing 2.18 shows the core.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.18 – kern_dup: take a reference, install the copy, then close what was there (kern_descrip.c lines 1086-1166)Source ↗
        oldfde = &fdp->fd_ofiles[old];
        oldfp = oldfde->fde_file;
        if (!fhold(oldfp))
                goto unlock;
⋮
        switch (mode) {
        case FDDUP_NORMAL:
        case FDDUP_FCNTL:
                if ((error = fdalloc(td, new, &new)) != 0) {
⋮
        case FDDUP_FIXED:
                if (new >= fdp->fd_nfiles) {
⋮
        newfde = &fdp->fd_ofiles[new];
        delfp = newfde->fde_file;
⋮
        fde_copy(oldfde, newfde);
⋮
        td->td_retval[0] = new;
⋮
        if (delfp != NULL) {
                (void) closefp(fdp, new, delfp, td, true, false);

fhold is the counterpart of INC sf_ref_count. Note the order in dup2: FreeBSD installs the new entry under the descriptor table lock, then drops the lock and closes the file that was previously at new (delfp), so another thread can never observe new as closed. MS-DOS $Dup2 closes first and duplicates second; with one program running at a time there is no observer.

The operations vector is how a read reaches the right code: fo_read calls fp->f_ops->fo_read (file.h lines 359-365), and for vnodes that is vn_io_fault from the table vnops (vfs_vnops.c lines 107-109). Study case 2.A follows this path to the disk.

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Per-process table JFT in the PSP, 20 bytes, relocatable (67h) filedesc -> fdescenttbl, starts at 20, grows
Entry contents 1-byte SFN or 0FFh pointer to struct file, capability rights, flags
System-wide open file SFT entry (59 bytes), fixed pool FILES= struct file, allocated on demand
Shared position sf_position in the SFT entry f_offset in struct file
Reference count sf_ref_count f_count (fhold/fdrop)
Per-file object none; directory sector and cluster cached in the SFT vnode, shared by all opens
Not inherited by children sf_no_inherit bit, per open file UF_FOCLOSE (close-on-fork) and UF_EXCLOSE (close-on-exec), per descriptor
dup2 close target, then duplicate duplicate, then close the old target, atomically

2.4 The FAT file system, implemented twice#

Both kernels can read and write the same FAT12 and FAT16 volumes. MS-DOS 4.00 implements FAT in assembly spread over FAT.ASM, ROM.ASM, DIR*.ASM, DISK*.ASM and BUF.ASM; FreeBSD implements it in C as one of many file systems behind the vnode interface, in sys/fs/msdosfs. The format is the same; the code shares nothing.

A FAT volume has four regions: reserved sectors (the boot sector with the BIOS Parameter Block, BPB), one or more copies of the File Allocation Table, the root directory, and the data area divided into clusters (DOSSYM.INC lines 79-99). The FAT has one entry per cluster; an entry holds the number of the next cluster of the same file, 0 for a free cluster, or an end-of-chain mark. Files are linked lists of clusters, and a directory entry holds the first cluster. The MS-DOS source states the FAT12 rule in one paragraph (Listing 2.19).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.19 – The FAT12 packing rule as documented in DOSSYM.INC (DOSSYM.INC lines 105-117)Source ↗
; The File Allocation Table uses a 12-bit entry for each allocation unit on
; the disk.  These entries are packed, two for every three bytes.  The contents
; of entry number N is found by 1) multiplying N by 1.5; 2) adding the result
; to the base address of the Allocation Table; 3) fetching the 16-bit word
; at this address; 4) If N was odd (so that N*1.5 was not an integer), shift
; the word right four bits; 5) mask to 12 bits (AND with 0FFF hex).  Entry
; number zero is used as an end-of-file trap in the OS and is passed to the
; BIOS to help determine disk format.  Entry 1 is reserved for future use.
; The first available allocation unit is assigned entry number two, and even
; though it is the first, is called cluster 2.  Entries greater than 0FF8H
; (12-bit fats) or 0FFF8H (16-bit fats) are end of file marks; entries of zero
; are unallocated.  Otherwise, the contents of a FAT entry is the number of
; the next cluster in the file.

Directory entries are 32 bytes in both implementations, but the reserved bytes 12-21 were later given meanings. Compare dir_entry in DIRENT.INC lines 28-40 with struct direntry in direntry.h lines 57-82:

Offset MS-DOS 4.00 dir_entry FreeBSD struct direntry
0 dir_name[11] deName[11]
11 dir_attr deAttributes
12 dir_codepg (word, "code page DOS 4.00") deLowerCase, deCHundredth
14 dir_extcluster (extended attributes) deCTime[2] (creation time)
16 dir_attr2, dir_pad[5] deCDate, deADate, deHighClust (FAT32)
22 dir_time deMTime
24 dir_date deMDate
26 dir_first deStartCluster
28 dir_size_l, dir_size_h deFileSize[4]

Each kernel keeps the geometry of a mounted volume in a structure built from the BPB: the Drive Parameter Block (dpb, DPB.INC lines 7-27) and struct msdosfsmount (msdosfsmount.h lines 77-122).

FAT12 or FAT16? Neither the MS-DOS 4.00 code nor msdosfs reads a "type" string. Both decide from the number of clusters, and both use the same threshold. MS-DOS compares dpb_max_cluster, defined as "Number of clusters on drive + 1" (DPB.INC line 17), with 4096-10 = 4086 (FAT.ASM lines 80-81, FAT.ASM lines 269-271). FreeBSD computes pm_maxcluster as the same quantity and compares it with CLUST_RSRVD & FAT12_MASK = 0xff6 = 4086 (Listing 2.20).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.20 – msdosfs chooses FAT12 or FAT16 from the cluster count (msdosfs_vfsops.c lines 699-721)Source ↗
        pmp->pm_maxcluster = (pmp->pm_HugeSectors - pmp->pm_firstcluster) /
            SecPerClust + 1;
        pmp->pm_fatsize = pmp->pm_FATsecs * DEV_BSIZE;
⋮
        if (pmp->pm_fatmask == 0) {
⋮
                if (pmp->pm_maxcluster < (CLUST_RSRVD & FAT12_MASK)) {
                        /*
                         * This will usually be a floppy disk. This size makes
                         * sure that one FAT entry will not be split across
                         * multiple blocks.
                         */
                        pmp->pm_fatmask = FAT12_MASK;
                        pmp->pm_fatmult = 3;
                        pmp->pm_fatdiv = 2;
                } else {
                        pmp->pm_fatmask = FAT16_MASK;
                        pmp->pm_fatmult = 2;
                        pmp->pm_fatdiv = 1;
                }

pm_fatmult/pm_fatdiv = 3/2 encode the 1.5 bytes per FAT12 entry for FATOFS (msdosfsmount.h line 135). Cluster to sector is the same formula in both (subtract 2, multiply by sectors per cluster, add the first data sector): FIGREC with shifts (ROM.ASM lines 539-564), cntobn in C (msdosfsmount.h lines 207-208). Both cache blocks: MS-DOS in its BUFFERS= sector buffers (header in BUFFER.INC lines 9-31, lookup in GETBUFFR, BUF.ASM lines 392-408), FreeBSD in the general buffer cache (bread/brelse). Study case 2.B compares the FAT12 decoding and the chain walk line by line.

2.5 Memory management#

The MS-DOS arena#

All memory that programs can obtain is one list of blocks, the arena. Each block is preceded by a 16-byte Memory Control Block (MCB, arena in the source, Listing 2.21) in the paragraph just below it: a block at segment S has its MCB at S-1. The signature is 4Dh ('M'), or 5Ah ('Z') for the last block; the owner is the owning program's PSP segment, 0 if free; the size is in paragraphs, header excluded. MS-DOS 4.00 also stores up to eight characters of the program name, filled in by EXEC (EXEC.ASM lines 648-667).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.21 – The memory control block (ARENA.INC lines 10-26)Source ↗
arena   STRUC
arena_signature     DB  ?               ; 4D for valid item, 5A for last item
arena_owner         DW  ?               ; owner of arena item
arena_size          DW  ?               ; size in paragraphs of item
arena_reserved      DB  3 DUP(?)        ; reserved
arena_name          DB  8 DUP(?)        ; owner file name
arena   ENDS
⋮
arena_owner_system  EQU 0               ; free block indication

arena_signature_normal  EQU 4Dh         ; valid signature, not end of arena
arena_signature_end     EQU 5Ah         ; valid signature, last block in arena

The first MCB's segment, arena_head, is the word just before SYSINITVAR, whose address function 52h returns in ES:BX (MSCONST.ASM lines 63-69, MISC.ASM lines 150-155): the first MCB is at the word ES:[BX-2]. arena_next computes next = current + size + 1, and check_signature rejects anything but 'M' or 'Z' (ALLOC.ASM lines 86-115).

$ALLOC (48h) scans the whole chain. It merges each free block with the free blocks after it (Coalesce, ALLOC.ASM lines 123-140) and remembers the first, the best (smallest sufficient) and the last fitting block (Listing 2.22). AllocMethod, set with function 58h (ALLOC.ASM lines 375-389), picks the candidate: 0 first fit, 1 best fit, larger values last fit, which returns the upper part of the block (ALLOC.ASM lines 242-252).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.22 – $ALLOC: coalesce, track first/best/last fit, pick by AllocMethod (ALLOC.ASM lines 207-264)Source ↗
alloc_free:
        CALL    coalesce                ; add following free block to current
        JC      alloc_err               ; IF error THEN GOTO err
        MOV     CX,DS:[arena_size]

⋮
        CMP     BX,CX                   ; IF BX > size of current block THEN
        JA      alloc_next              ;   GOTO next

        CMP     [FirstArena],0
        JNZ     alloc_best
        MOV     [FirstArena],DS         ; save first one found
alloc_best:
        CMP     [BestArena],0
        JZ      alloc_make_best         ; initial best
        PUSH    ES
        MOV     ES,[BestArena]
        CMP     ES:[arena_size],CX      ; is size of best larger than found?
        POP     ES
        JBE     alloc_last
alloc_make_best:
        MOV     [BestArena],DS          ; assign best
alloc_last:
        MOV     [LastArena],DS          ; assign last
        JMP     alloc_next
⋮
alloc_do_split:
        CMP     BYTE PTR [AllocMethod], 1
        JA      alloc_do_split_high
        MOV     DS,[FirstArena]
        JB      alloc_get_size
        MOV     DS,[BestArena]

Freeing (49h) only sets the owner to 0 (ALLOC.ASM lines 346-361); merging waits for the next scan. SETBLOCK (4Ah) resizes in place. A request that is too large fails with error 8 and the largest free size in BX, so BX = FFFFh means "how much is there?" (EXEC asks exactly that, EXEC.ASM lines 357-369). A bad signature met while walking the chain makes 48h (and therefore EXEC) fail with error 7, error_arena_trashed (ERROR.INC lines 29-31); 4Ah checks only its own MCB and the one after it, and 49h only its own, failing with error 9, error_invalid_block. One stray store into an MCB is enough to stop every later program from loading, a classic MS-DOS failure. At exit, arena_free_process frees every block owned by the dying PSP (ALLOC.ASM lines 57-78); blocks SYSINIT keeps get the "impossible owner" 8 (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 1688-1693).

FreeBSD: address spaces, map entries, page faults, kernel malloc#

A FreeBSD process never asks for physical memory. Its virtual address space is a struct vmspace whose vm_map (vm_map.h lines 203-220) is a sorted set of vm_map_entry records. Each maps [start, end) with a protection onto a VM object (file, anonymous memory, device) at an offset (Listing 2.23). Entries live in a splay tree whose max_free fields let mmap find gaps quickly.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.23 – A virtual memory map entry (vm_map.h lines 100-117)Source ↗
struct vm_map_entry {
        struct vm_map_entry *left;      /* left child or previous entry */
        struct vm_map_entry *right;     /* right child or next entry */
        vm_offset_t start;              /* start address */
        vm_offset_t end;                /* end address */
        vm_offset_t next_read;          /* vaddr of the next sequential read */
        vm_size_t max_free;             /* max free space in subtree */
        union vm_map_object object;     /* object I point to */
        vm_ooffset_t offset;            /* offset into object */
        vm_eflags_t eflags;             /* map entry flags */
        vm_prot_t protection;           /* protection code */
        vm_prot_t max_protection;       /* maximum protection */
        vm_inherit_t inheritance;       /* inheritance */
        uint8_t read_ahead;             /* pages in the read-ahead window */
        int wired_count;                /* can be paged if = 0 */
        struct ucred *cred;             /* tmp storage for creator ref */
        struct thread *wiring_thread;
};

An entry allocates no physical memory. Pages arrive on first touch: the page fault goes to trap_pfault (trap.c line 779), then vm_fault_trap (trap.c line 916, vm_fault.c lines 742-760), then vm_fault, which finds the entry, gets or creates the page in the object and enters it into the page table. No entry means SIGSEGV (vm_fault.c lines 765-771). On MS-DOS a bad pointer just reads or writes whatever is there. Inside the kernel, malloc(9) serves small requests from per-size UMA zones and large ones from the kernel memory allocator (kern_malloc.c lines 657-691).

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Unit paragraph (16 bytes) page (4 KB) for mappings; bytes for malloc(9)
Bookkeeping MCB in front of each block, linked by size vm_map_entry tree per process, separate from the memory
Owner PSP segment in the MCB the process whose vm_map holds the entry
Placement policy first, best or last fit (58h) address chosen by vm_map_find/ASLR; physical pages chosen at fault time
Release owner = 0; lazy coalescing unmap; pages freed when objects lose references
Corruption error 7, "arena trashed" impossible from user mode; kernel bugs panic
Protection none per entry: read/write/execute

2.6 Programs and processes#

MS-DOS EXEC#

Function 4Bh ($Exec, EXEC.ASM lines 132-149) loads and starts a program in one call (AL=0; AL=1 loads without running, for debuggers; AL=3 loads an overlay). It:

  1. opens the file and refuses devices (EXEC.ASM lines 182-219);
  2. copies the environment (the parent's unless the parameter block names another) into a new block, followed by a word 1 and the program name as passed (EXEC.ASM lines 225-278);
  3. reads the first 1Ah bytes of header (EXEC.ASM lines 104-117): if they start with MZ (exe_valid_signature = 5A4Dh as a little-endian word, EXE.INC lines 70-71), or with the older ZM (exe_valid_old_signature = 4D5Ah), the file is an .EXE; otherwise, or if fewer than 1Ah bytes could be read, it is a .COM memory image, whatever its extension (EXEC.ASM lines 280-309);
  4. allocates memory: the largest free block for a .COM (EXEC.ASM lines 561-570), the image plus exe_min_BSS to exe_max_BSS paragraphs for an .EXE (EXEC.ASM lines 357-401);
  5. reads the image and, for an .EXE, adds the load segment to every word listed in the relocation table (EXEC.ASM lines 515-529), since the linker produced it for segment 0;
  6. builds the PSP with $Dup_PDB, which also duplicates the handles, and fills in the environment segment, the default FCBs at 5Ch/6Ch and the command tail at 80h (EXEC.ASM lines 674-727);
  7. makes the caller's return address the child's terminate address and jumps to the child (Listing 2.24).

A .COM program starts with CS = DS = ES = SS = PSP, IP = 100h and a zero word on top of the stack, so a final RET reaches the INT 20h at PSP offset 0 (EXEC.ASM lines 601-612).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.24 – Starting the child: InDOS = 0, child's stack, far return to the entry point (EXEC.ASM lines 778-806)Source ↗
exec_go:
        LDS     SI,DWORD PTR exec_init_IP   ; get entry point
        LES     DI,DWORD PTR exec_init_SP   ; new stack
        MOV     AX,ES
;
; DS:SI points to entry point
; AX:DI points to initial stack
; DX has PDB pointer
; BX has initial AX value
;
        CLI
        MOV     BYTE PTR INDOS,0
        ASSUME  SS:NOTHING
        MOV     SS,AX                   ; set up user's stack
        MOV     SP,DI                   ; and SP
        STI
        PUSH    DS                      ; fake long call to entry
        PUSH    SI
        MOV     ES,DX                   ; set up proper seg registers
        MOV     DS,DX
        MOV     AX,BX                   ; set up proper AX
⋮
        RET
EndProc exec_long_ret

The parent never leaves its INT 21h call. Its register frame stays on its stack, recorded in its PDB_User_stack (Listing 2.3); EXEC copies its return CS:IP into the child's PDB_Exit and the INT 22h vector (EXEC.ASM lines 744-755), clears InDOS and jumps. When the child exits (4Ch, 00h, INT 20h or 31h), $EXIT/$ABORT (PROC.ASM lines 129-184) store the exit code and restore the INT 22h-24h vectors, and reset_environment frees the child, makes the parent current, reloads the parent's stack and IRETs to the instruction after the parent's INT 21h (Study case 2.D). The parent reads the code with 4Dh (PROC.ASM lines 62-67). A TSR exits with 31h, $Keep_process (PROC.ASM lines 81-106): its block is shrunk, and exit type 3 makes reset_environment keep its memory and handles (CTRLC.ASM lines 663-673), so its hooked interrupt handlers stay alive.

FreeBSD fork, execve, exit and wait#

FreeBSD splits "create a process" from "run a program". fork (Listing 2.25) asks fork1 for a new process with RFFDG | RFPROC: a new process (RFPROC) with a copy of the descriptor table (RFFDG).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.25 – fork(2) is fork1 with "new process, copy the fd table" (kern_fork.c lines 99-114)Source ↗
int
sys_fork(struct thread *td, struct fork_args *uap)
{
        struct fork_req fr;
        int error, pid;

        bzero(&fr, sizeof(fr));
        fr.fr_flags = RFFDG | RFPROC;
        fr.fr_pidp = &pid;
        error = fork1(td, &fr);
        if (error == 0) {
                td->td_retval[0] = pid;
                td->td_retval[1] = 0;
        }
        return (error);
}

fork1 creates the struct proc and the first thread, copies the address space with vmspace_fork (kern_fork.c lines 1074-1079), which clones each inheritable map entry as copy-on-write instead of copying pages (vm_map.c lines 4546-4566), and do_fork copies the descriptor table with fdcopy (kern_fork.c lines 469-475). The child is a copy of the parent that resumes from the same system call. The two returns differ only in the trap frame: the child gets %rax = 0, carry clear, and %rdx = 1 (Listing 2.26).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.26 – The child's return value from fork (vm_machdep.c lines 303-311)Source ↗
void
x86_set_fork_retval(struct thread *td)
{
        struct trapframe *frame = td->td_frame;

        frame->tf_rax = 0;              /* Child returns zero */
        frame->tf_rflags &= ~PSL_C;     /* success */
        frame->tf_rdx = 1;              /* System V emulation */
}

execve then replaces the program in the current process. sys_execve copies the path, arguments and environment into the kernel (kern_exec.c lines 224-240), and do_execve opens the file, maps its first page (kern_exec.c line 566) and offers it to each image activator in turn (Listing 2.27). For an ELF binary the activator in imgact_elf.c (imgact_elf.c lines 1102-1121) discards the old address space (exec_new_vmspace, imgact_elf.c line 1324) and maps every PT_LOAD segment (imgact_elf.c lines 743-762). Mapping, not reading: the pages arrive later by page faults. Then do_execve closes close-on-exec descriptors (kern_exec.c lines 759-766) and sets the initial registers (kern_exec.c lines 959-960).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.27 – Trying each image activator (kern_exec.c lines 658-674)Source ↗
        /*
         *      Loop through the list of image activators, calling each one.
         *      An activator returns -1 if there is no match, 0 on success,
         *      and an error otherwise.
         */
        error = -1;
        for (i = 0; error == -1 && execsw[i]; ++i) {
                if (execsw[i]->ex_imgact == NULL)
                        continue;
                error = (*execsw[i]->ex_imgact)(imgp);
        }

        if (error) {
                if (error == -1)
                        error = ENOEXEC;
                goto exec_fail_dealloc;
        }

_exit ends in exit1 (kern_exit.c line 225), which closes the descriptors (fdescfree, kern_exit.c line 403), releases the address space (kern_exit.c line 421), turns the process into a zombie, signals the parent with SIGCHLD and wakes it (kern_exit.c lines 685-709). The parent collects the status with wait4/waitpid, implemented by kern_wait6 (kern_exit.c line 1393).

Why MS-DOS has no fork. fork duplicates an address space. A running real-mode program holds absolute segment values in its registers, on its stack and in its data (for an .EXE the loader patched them in), so a byte-for-byte copy at another address would still point into the parent; and without paging the copy cannot be placed at the same address. There is also only one CPU context: DOS has no scheduler that could run parent and child alternately. MS-DOS keeps the parent suspended inside the EXEC call and resumes it when the child exits, which gives the familiar system()-like behaviour without any of the machinery.

2.7 Device drivers#

An MS-DOS device driver is a memory image that begins with a device header (Listing 2.28): a far link to the next driver, an attribute word, the offsets of two entry points called strategy and interrupt, and an 8-byte name (character devices such as CON, PRN, NUL) or a unit count (block devices, which get drive letters). The kernel talks to a driver by building a request header (the "packet") with a length, a unit, a command code and a status word, followed by command-specific fields. Command codes include 0 init, 1 media check, 2 build BPB, 4 read, 8 write, 13 open and 14 close (DEVSYM.INC lines 113-146).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.28 – Device header and static request header (DEVSYM.INC lines 6-102)Source ↗
SYSDEV         STRUC
SDEVNEXT       DD    ?              ;POINTER TO NEXT DEVICE HEADER
SDEVATT        DW    ?              ;ATTRIBUTES OF THE DEVICE
SDEVSTRAT      DW    ?              ;STRATEGY ENTRY POINT
SDEVINT        DW    ?              ;INTERRUPT ENTRY POINT
SDEVNAME       DB    8 DUP (?)      ;NAME OF DEVICE (ONLY FIRST BYTE USED FOR BLOCK)
SYSDEV         ENDS
⋮
SRHEAD         STRUC
REQLEN         DB    ?              ;LENGTH IN BYTES OF REQUEST BLOCK
REQUNIT        DB    ?              ;DEVICE UNIT NUMBER
REQFUNC        DB    ?              ;TYPE OF REQUEST
REQSTAT        DW    ?              ;STATUS WORD
               DB    8 DUP(?)       ;RESERVED FOR QUEUE LINKS
SRHEAD         ENDS

DEVIOCALL (Listing 2.29) makes every driver call: it far-calls the strategy routine with ES:BX pointing at the packet, then immediately far-calls the interrupt routine, then reads the status. The two-step interface would let a driver queue requests; MS-DOS 4.00 never takes advantage of that, so in practice the strategy routine saves the packet address and the interrupt routine does the work. The packet for a read is built by SETREAD (DEV.ASM lines 509-548) in the single global DEVCALL buffer.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.29 – Calling a driver: strategy, then interrupt (DEV.ASM lines 442-493)Source ↗
        procedure   DEVIOCALL,NEAR
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING

        Assert  ISSFT,<DS,SI>,"DevIOCall"
        LDS     SI,[SI.sf_devptr]

        entry   DEVIOCALL2

        EnterCrit   critDevice
⋮
chardev2:                              ;AN000;
; As above only DS:SI points to device header on entry, and DS:SI is preserved
        MOV     AX,[SI.SDEVSTRAT]
        MOV     WORD PTR [CALLDEVAD],AX
        MOV     WORD PTR [CALLDEVAD+2],DS
        CALL    DWORD PTR [CALLDEVAD]
        MOV     AX,[SI.SDEVINT]
        MOV     WORD PTR [CALLDEVAD],AX
        CALL    DWORD PTR [CALLDEVAD]
        CALL    VIRREAD                 ;AN000;LB. move data from SC to buffer
        JC      chardev2                ;AN000;LB. bad sector or exceeds max sec
dev_exit:
        LeaveCrit   critDevice
        return
EndProc DEVIOCALL

The simplest MS-DOS driver lives inside the DOS data segment: the header of NUL, the first entry of the device chain, is part of SYSINITVAR (MSCONST.ASM lines 79-84): its strategy entry just sets the "done" bit and its interrupt entry just returns (MS_CODE.ASM lines 48-53). Drivers loaded with DEVICE= (Module 1) are linked into the same chain.

FreeBSD character devices are described by a struct cdevsw (Listing 2.30): one function pointer per operation, no packets. /dev/null and /dev/zero are in null.c (Listing 2.31), which is compiled into every kernel (files line 2564) and registered as a module (null.c line 250); its load handler creates the devices with make_dev_credf (null.c lines 189-202), and devfs makes them visible under /dev.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.30 – The character device switch (conf.h lines 197-214)Source ↗
struct cdevsw {
        int                     d_version;
        u_int                   d_flags;
        const char              *d_name;
        d_open_t                *d_open;
        d_fdopen_t              *d_fdopen;
        d_close_t               *d_close;
        d_read_t                *d_read;
        d_write_t               *d_write;
        d_ioctl_t               *d_ioctl;
        d_poll_t                *d_poll;
        d_mmap_t                *d_mmap;
        d_strategy_t            *d_strategy;
        void                    *d_spare0;
        d_kqfilter_t            *d_kqfilter;
        d_purge_t               *d_purge;
        d_mmap_single_t         *d_mmap_single;
FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.31 – /dev/null: discard writes by consuming the uio (null.c lines 83-117)Source ↗
static struct cdevsw null_cdevsw = {
        .d_version =    D_VERSION,
        .d_read =       (d_read_t *)nullop,
        .d_write =      null_write,
        .d_ioctl =      null_ioctl,
        .d_kqfilter =   kqfilter,
        .d_name =       "null",
};
⋮
/* ARGSUSED */
static int
null_write(struct cdev *dev __unused, struct uio *uio, int flags __unused)
{
        uio->uio_resid = 0;

        return (0);
}

File systems do not call disk drivers directly. FreeBSD routes block I/O through GEOM, a stack of layers (partitions, mirrors, encryption) between file systems and disk drivers: msdosfs hands a struct buf to g_vfs_strategy, which turns it into a struct bio for g_io_request (geom_vfs.c lines 185-229). Strategy keeps the same meaning in both systems, "here is an I/O request, carry it out": the MS-DOS strategy entry, d_strategy in cdevsw, VOP_STRATEGY (msdosfs_strategy, Study case 2.A) and bop_strategy for buffer objects.

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Driver description device header in the driver image struct cdevsw; GEOM classes for disks
Request packet (request header) in memory direct function call with uio, or struct bio
Entry points strategy + interrupt, far calls one function per operation
Registration DEVICE= at boot; linked list of headers make_dev, kernel modules at any time
Naming 8-character name, valid in every directory node under /dev (devfs)
Null device header inside MSDOS.SYS data null.c, compiled in, registered as a module

2.8 Concurrency and interrupts#

MS-DOS is single-threaded. Hardware interrupt handlers (BIOS or TSRs) run at any moment on whatever stack is current; DOS protects its own short sequences with CLI/STI (the stack switch in Listing 2.3, the vector store in Listing 2.1) and everything longer with InDOS. The source also marks critical sections with EnterCrit/LeaveCrit (DOSMAC.INC lines 362-370) for disk buffers, devices, memory and SFTs. They cost almost nothing, because each handler starts with RET (Listing 2.32); the sharer patches that byte to PUSH AX (the patch list CritPatch, CONST2.ASM lines 78-93), which turns every critical section into an INT 2Ah request (AX = 8000h or 8100h plus the section number) that a network or multitasking layer can hook.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.32 – Critical sections that are a single RET until someone patches them (CRIT.ASM lines 38-56)Source ↗
;
;   Each handler must leave everything untouched; including flags!
;
;   Sleaze for time savings:  first instruction is a return.  This is patched
;   by the sharer to be a PUSH AX to complete the correct routines.
;
Procedure   EcritDisk,NEAR
        public  EcritMem
        public  EcritSFT
ECritMEM    LABEL   NEAR
ECritSFT    LABEL   NEAR
        RET
;       PUSH    AX
        fmt     TypSect,LevReq,<"PDB $x entering $x">,<CurrentPDB,sect>
        MOV     AX,8000h+critDisk
        INT     int_ibm
        POP     AX
        return
EndProc EcritDisk

FreeBSD runs system calls, interrupt threads and kernel threads on many CPUs at once, so every shared structure has a lock. Taking a free mutex(9) is one atomic compare-and-swap of the owner field from MTX_UNOWNED to the current thread (Listing 2.33); otherwise the thread spins or sleeps in _mtx_lock_sleep. A spin mutex first calls spinlock_enter, which disables interrupts on this CPU (machdep.c lines 1702-1716): the descendant of CLI, per CPU and nestable. Locks seen earlier: the descriptor table lock (FILEDESC_XLOCK, Listing 2.18), the vnode lock (vn_lock in vn_read, vfs_vnops.c lines 1247-1268) and the map lock (Study case 2.C).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.33 – Lock fast path: one atomic compare-and-set (mutex.h lines 237-246)Source ↗
/* Lock a normal mutex. */
#define __mtx_lock(mp, tid, opts, file, line) __extension__ ({          \
        uintptr_t _tid = (uintptr_t)(tid);                              \
        uintptr_t _v = MTX_UNOWNED;                                     \
                                                                        \
        if (__predict_false(LOCKSTAT_PROFILE_ENABLED(adaptive__acquire) ||\
            !_mtx_obtain_lock_fetch((mp), &_v, _tid)))                  \
                _mtx_lock_sleep((mp), _v, (opts), (file), (line));      \
        (void)0; /* ensure void type for expression */                  \
})
MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Execution contexts in the kernel one DOS call at a time; interrupt handlers many threads on many CPUs; interrupt threads
Short critical section CLI … STI spin mutex (spinlock_enter disables interrupts)
Long critical section InDOS (callers must check it) sleep mutexes, sx locks, rangelocks
Hooks for multitasking EnterCrit stubs patched to INT 2Ah; INT 28h idle built in: scheduler, sleep queues
Re-entrancy no (one set of stacks, global state) yes (per-thread kernel stack, per-thread state)

Study cases#

Study case 2.A: One read, end to end#

Goal. Follow one read of a FAT file from the calling instruction to the disk driver and back, in both kernels, and name the source line of every hop. On MS-DOS the program executes INT 21h AH=3Fh on a file of the lab floppy (drive A:); on FreeBSD a program calls read(2) on the same file after the floppy image has been attached with mdconfig and mounted with mount_msdosfs (Exercise 2.3).

Walk-through. Sections 2.2 and 2.3 already took both calls to the point where the kernel holds the open-file object. From there the paths look like this:

Hop MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
1. Handler $READ: handle -> SFT into ThisSFT, normalise DS:DX into DMAADD, call DOS_Read (HANDLE.ASM lines 343-422) sys_read builds a uio; kern_readv gets the struct file with fget_read (sys_generic.c lines 281-293)
2. Generic file layer DOS_READ: refuse write-only opens, SETUP, then device or local disk file (DISK.ASM lines 160-218) dofileread -> fo_read -> vn_io_fault -> vn_read: lock the vnode, VOP_READ (sys_generic.c lines 344-383, vfs_vnops.c lines 1213-1278)
3. FAT layer DISKREAD: clamp to EOF, split into partial first sector, whole sectors, partial last sector (BREAKDOWN), find the cluster (FNDCLUS) (DISK2.ASM lines 453-485) msdosfs_read: loop over clusters, bread each one (Listing 2.34)
4. Cache partial sectors through the buffer pool: BUFRD -> BUFSEC -> GETBUFFR (ROM.ASM lines 212-285); whole sectors with DREAD straight into the user's buffer, then any dirty cached copy of those sectors is copied over them (DISK2.ASM lines 654-691) breadn_flags looks the block up and, if absent, starts I/O with bstrategy and sleeps in bufwait (vfs_bio.c lines 2235-2302)
5. Logical to physical cluster to sector with FIGREC (Section 2.4) msdosfs_strategy calls pcbmap to turn the file block into a volume block, then BO_STRATEGY on the device (msdosfs_vnops.c lines 1881-1920)
6. Driver call DREAD -> DSKREAD: SETREAD packet, DEVIOCALL2 (DISK.ASM lines 869-884, DISK2.ASM lines 108-118, Listing 2.29); on error INT 24h via HARDERRRW g_vfs_strategy -> g_io_request -> GEOM -> md(4) (geom_vfs.c lines 185-229)
7. Copy to user REP MOVSW from the buffer to DMAADD (ROM.ASM lines 258-267) vn_io_fault_uiomove -> copyout (Listing 2.34)
8. Return SYS_RET_OK, AX = bytes (HANDLE.ASM lines 419-421) td_retval[0] = bytes, cpu_set_syscall_retval
FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.34 – msdosfs_read: one cluster-sized buffer per iteration (msdosfs_vnops.c lines 556-603)Source ↗
        do {
                if (uio->uio_offset >= dep->de_FileSize)
                        break;
                lbn = de_cluster(pmp, uio->uio_offset);
                rablock = lbn + 1;
                blsize = pmp->pm_bpcluster;
                on = uio->uio_offset & pmp->pm_crbomask;
⋮
                } else if (de_cn2off(pmp, rablock) >= dep->de_FileSize) {
                        error = bread(vp, lbn, blsize, NOCRED, &bp);
                } else if ((vp->v_mount->mnt_flag & MNT_NOCLUSTERR) == 0) {
                        error = cluster_read(vp, dep->de_FileSize, lbn, blsize,
                            NOCRED, on + uio->uio_resid, seqcount, 0, &bp);
                } else if (seqcount > 1) {
                        rasize = blsize;
                        error = breadn(vp, lbn,
                            blsize, &rablock, &rasize, 1, NOCRED, &bp);
                } else {
                        error = bread(vp, lbn, blsize, NOCRED, &bp);
                }
⋮
                diff = pmp->pm_bpcluster - on;
                n = diff > uio->uio_resid ? uio->uio_resid : diff;
                diff = dep->de_FileSize - uio->uio_offset;
                if (diff < n)
                        n = diff;
                diff = blsize - bp->b_resid;
                if (diff < n)
                        n = diff;
                error = vn_io_fault_uiomove(bp->b_data + on, (int) n, uio);
                brelse(bp);
        } while (error == 0 && uio->uio_resid > 0 && n != 0);

What to notice.

  • MS-DOS performs the whole read synchronously: DEVIOCALL returns when the driver is done. FreeBSD starts the I/O in bstrategy and sleeps in bufwait; other threads run until the GEOM completion wakes it.
  • MS-DOS reads whole sectors straight into the caller's memory and patches in newer dirty copies; msdosfs reads whole clusters into the shared buffer cache and copies out the requested part. One saves buffer space and a copy, the other lets every reader share cached data.
  • MS-DOS walks the FAT chain before the transfer (FNDCLUS); msdosfs maps lazily at read time (pcbmap): in msdosfs_bmap for clustered reads, the default, or in the strategy routine when the block's disk address is still unknown, once per uncached block.
MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Layers between system call and driver 4 (handle, DOS_READ, DISKREAD, buffer/driver) 7 or more (syscall, file, vnode, msdosfs, buffer cache, GEOM, driver)
Waiting for the disk busy, inside the driver thread sleeps; other threads run
Where data lands first the user's buffer (whole sectors) the buffer cache
Who maps file offset to sector DOS (FNDCLUS, FIGREC) before I/O msdosfs (pcbmap, via msdosfs_bmap or the strategy routine) at read time

Discussion questions.

  1. Why can MS-DOS afford to bypass its cache for whole-sector reads, and what would break if it did not patch in the dirty cached sectors afterwards?
  2. FreeBSD calls pcbmap from msdosfs_strategy only when b_blkno == b_lblkno. What does that test mean, and why does it make repeated reads of the same block cheap?
  3. Count the times the data is copied in each system for a 100-byte read at offset 0.

Study case 2.B: Decoding FAT12 and walking a cluster chain#

Goal. Decode FAT12 entries by hand and in both implementations, and compare how each kernel follows a chain of clusters.

A worked example. Suppose the first nine bytes of the FAT are F0 FF FF 03 40 00 FF 0F 00. Entries 0 and 1 are reserved (FF0, FFF). A file starting at cluster 2 occupies clusters 2, 3, 4:

Cluster n byte offset n*3/2 16-bit little-endian word n odd? entry
2 3 4003h no: AND 0FFFh 003 (next is 3)
3 4 0040h yes: SHR 4 004 (next is 4)
4 6 0FFFh no: AND 0FFFh FFF (end of chain, >= FF8)

MS-DOS. MAPCLUSTER (Listing 2.35) computes the byte offset n/2 + n (FAT16: n + n), reads the FAT sector that holds it into a buffer (GETBUFFRB) and returns a pointer to the entry; the zero flag says whether the entry is in the high 12 bits. An entry that starts in the last byte of a sector spans two sectors, so MAPCLUSTER copies its two bytes into CLUSSAVE and points there (CLUSSPLIT = 1). UNPACK (Listing 2.36) then shifts or masks.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.35 – MAPCLUSTER: byte offset n*1.5, buffered FAT sector, entry split across two sectors (FAT.ASM lines 261-351)Source ↗
        procedure   MAPCLUSTER,NEAR
⋮
        MOV     AX,BX                   ; AX = BX
        MOV     CX,4096-10
        CMP     ES:[BP.dpb_max_cluster],CX  ; MZ 16 bit fat?
        JAE     Map16                   ; MZ yes, do 16 bit algorithm
        SHR     AX,1                    ; AX = BX/2
Map16:                                  ; MZ skip prev => AX=2*BX
        XOR     DI,DI                   ; >32mb     fat                         ;AN000;
        ADD     AX,BX                   ; AX = 1.5*fat = byte offset in fat
        ADC     DI,0                    ; >32mb     fat                         ;AN000;
⋮
        LDS     SI,[CURBUF]
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        LEA     DI,[SI.BufInSiz]
        ADD     DI,AX
        CMP     AX,CX
        JNZ     MAPRET
        MOV     AL,[DI]
        Context DS
        INC     BYTE PTR [CLUSSPLIT]
        MOV     BYTE PTR [CLUSSAVE],AL
⋮
MAPRET:
        RestoreReg  <DX,CX,BX>
        XOR     AX,AX                   ; MZ allow shift to clear carry
        CMP     ES:[BP.dpb_max_cluster],4096-10 ; MZ is this 16-bit fat?
        JAE     MapSet                  ; MZ no, set flags
        MOV     AX,BX
MapSet:
        TEST    AL,1                    ; set zero flag if not on boundary
        RestoreReg  <AX>
        return
MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.36 – UNPACK: shift odd entries right by 4, mask to 12 bits (FAT.ASM lines 108-136)Source ↗
        procedure   UNPACK,NEAR
⋮
        CMP     BX,ES:[BP.dpb_max_cluster]
        JA      HURTFAT
        CALL    MAPCLUSTER
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        jc      DoContext
        MOV     DI,[DI]
        JNZ     High12                  ; MZ if high 12 bits, go get 'em
        MOV     SI,ES:[BP.dpb_max_cluster]  ; MZ is this 16-bit fat?
        CMP     SI,4096-10
        JB      Unpack12                ; MZ No, go 'AND' off bits
        OR      DI,DI                   ; MZ set zero condition code, clears carry
        JMP     SHORT DoContext         ; MZ go do context

High12:
        SHR     DI,1
        SHR     DI,1
        SHR     DI,1
        SHR     DI,1
Unpack12:
        AND     DI,0FFFH                ; Clears carry
DoContext:
        PUSH    SS
        POP     DS
        return

FreeBSD. fatentry (Listing 2.37) does the same with FATOFS, getushort (a little-endian 16-bit load, bpb.h lines 95-97) and a shift for odd clusters. Note the & where one expects && on line 522: it works because FAT12() evaluates to 0 or 1. The split-entry problem is avoided rather than handled: for FAT12 the FAT is read in blocks of 3 * 512 bytes (msdosfs_vfsops.c lines 735-741), which hold exactly 1024 entries, so no entry ever straddles a block (fatblock, msdosfs_fat.c lines 87-110).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.37 – fatentry, FAT_GET: the same three steps in C (msdosfs_fat.c lines 510-528)Source ↗
        byteoffset = FATOFS(pmp, cn);
        fatblock(pmp, byteoffset, &bn, &bsize, &bo);
        error = bread(pmp->pm_devvp, bn, bsize, NOCRED, &bp);
        if (error) {
                return (error);
        }

        if (function & FAT_GET) {
                if (FAT32(pmp))
                        readcn = getulong(bp->b_data + bo);
                else
                        readcn = getushort(bp->b_data + bo);
                if (FAT12(pmp) & (cn & 1))
                        readcn >>= 4;
                readcn &= pmp->pm_fatmask;
                /* map reserved FAT entries to same values for all FATs */
                if ((readcn | ~pmp->pm_fatmask) >= CLUST_RSRVD)
                        readcn |= ~pmp->pm_fatmask;
                *oldcontents = readcn;

Walking a chain. pcbmap (msdosfs_fat.c lines 190-235) maps a file-relative cluster number to a volume cluster by following the chain from the start, re-reading the FAT block only when the entry is in a different block. Both kernels cache their position so that sequential reads do not restart from the first cluster: MS-DOS keeps the last cluster and its position in the SFT (sf_lstclus, sf_cluspos, used by FNDCLUS, ROM.ASM lines 84-114); msdosfs keeps a small per-file FAT cache consulted by fc_lookup (msdosfs_fat.c lines 185-191). End of chain is any value at or above FF8h for MS-DOS (IsEof, which also accepts FF0h, FAT.ASM lines 77-95); msdosfs maps all reserved values to 32-bit constants first so one test (MSDOSFSEOF, fat.h line 82) serves FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32.

What to notice. The format fixes every number (1.5-byte offset, odd/even rule, threshold 4086), so both agree on them. MS-DOS optimises cycles (it avoids a DIV for 512-byte sectors, FAT.ASM lines 279-301) and handles the rare split entry with special code; FreeBSD picks a block size that makes the special case impossible and uses portable little-endian loads.

MS-DOS 4.00 (FAT.ASM) FreeBSD (msdosfs_fat.c)
Byte offset SHR AX,1 / ADD AX,BX FATOFS: cn * 3 / 2
Read the FAT GETBUFFRB into a DOS buffer bread of a FAT block on the device vnode
Entry across a boundary CLUSSPLIT/CLUSSAVE special case impossible: block = 3 sectors
Odd entry SHR DI,1 four times cn >>= 4
End of chain IsEof: >= FF8h (or = FF0h) MSDOSFSEOF after normalising reserved values
Position cache sf_lstclus, sf_cluspos in the SFT per-denode FAT cache (fc_lookup)

Discussion questions.

  1. Which cluster number is the first whose FAT12 entry starts in the last byte of the first FAT sector? Show that MAPCLUSTER takes the CLUSSPLIT path for it.
  2. Why would a block size of 2 sectors not work for msdosfs' trick, while 3 does?
  3. IsEof treats FF0h as end of chain. Read the comment and explain the compatibility problem it solves.

Study case 2.C: Walking the memory map#

Goal. List all memory blocks of a running MS-DOS system and all mappings of a FreeBSD process, and relate each line to the kernel structure that produced it.

MS-DOS. In the lab, boot the MS-DOS 4.00 image and run DEBUG. Assemble a call to function 52h, run it to the breakpoint and read the registers:

Terminal
-a 100
xxxx:0100 mov ah,52
xxxx:0102 int 21
xxxx:0104 int 3
xxxx:0105
-g=100

DEBUG addresses take plain hexadecimal numbers, so read ES and BX from the register display, compute BX-2 with DEBUG's h command, which prints the sum and the difference of two numbers (HEXADD in the command table, DEBUG.ASM lines 1003-1010), and dump the word with d <ES>:<BX-2> l2. That word is arena_head, the first MCB segment. Dump the MCB with d <segment>:0 l10, decode signature, owner, size and name using Listing 2.21, compute the next segment as segment + size + 1, and repeat until the signature is 5Ah. You are doing by hand what arena_free_process does in a loop (ALLOC.ASM lines 57-78). Expect blocks owned by 8 (system), by COMMAND.COM's PSP (its program and its environment) and by DEBUG's PSP; note who owns the last ('Z') block. Exercise 2.1 automates the walk.

FreeBSD. Run procstat -v $$ in a shell of the FreeBSD VM. Each output line is one vm_map_entry: procstat asks the kernel through the kern.proc.vmmap sysctl, whose handler walks the map with VM_MAP_ENTRY_FOREACH under a read lock (Listing 2.38). The START/END columns are entry->start/entry->end, PRT is entry->protection, TP the type of the backing object and PATH the file for vnode-backed entries (the column list is in procstat(1)).

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 2.38 – The kernel side of procstat -v: one record per map entry (kern_proc.c lines 2649-2692)Source ↗
        map = &vm->vm_map;
        vm_map_lock_read(map);
        VM_MAP_ENTRY_FOREACH(entry, map) {
                if (entry->eflags & MAP_ENTRY_IS_SUB_MAP)
                        continue;

                addr = entry->end;
⋮
                kve->kve_start = entry->start;
                kve->kve_end = entry->end;
                kve->kve_offset += entry->offset;

                if (entry->protection & VM_PROT_READ)
                        kve->kve_protection |= KVME_PROT_READ;
                if (entry->protection & VM_PROT_WRITE)
                        kve->kve_protection |= KVME_PROT_WRITE;
                if (entry->protection & VM_PROT_EXECUTE)

What to notice. The MCB chain lives inside the memory it describes: any program can read or damage it, and chain order is physical order. The FreeBSD map is per-process metadata in kernel memory, sorted by virtual address; physical pages are reached through VM objects and page tables, so adjacent entries may be backed by pages anywhere in RAM.

MCB chain vm_map
Scope whole machine one process
Ordered by physical address (chain order) virtual address (tree)
Stored in front of each block, in ordinary memory kernel memory, behind a lock
Per block signature, owner, size, name start, end, protection, object, offset, flags
Walk segment + size + 1 until 'Z' VM_MAP_ENTRY_FOREACH
Tool DEBUG and function 52h procstat -v, sysctl kern.proc.vmmap

Discussion questions.

  1. COMMAND.COM owns at least two blocks. Which one holds the environment, and how can you tell from the PSP (Listing 2.14)?
  2. Why does procstat -v show several entries for one shared library?
  3. What would a DOS program have to do to "hide" from an MCB walker, and why is the equivalent impossible for a FreeBSD process with respect to procstat -v?

Study case 2.D: EXEC versus fork and execve#

Goal. Compare what a new program inherits from its parent, and how the parent learns that the child has finished.

Handles. $Dup_PDB, called by EXEC, copies the parent's PSP and then walks the 20 JFT slots (Listing 2.39): a handle is inherited unless the SFT entry has sf_no_inherit or is a network FCB handle, in which case the child's slot gets 0FFh. FreeBSD's fdcopy (kern_descrip.c lines 2551-2576) copies every descriptor whose file is passable and not marked close-on-fork, taking a reference with fhold; execve later closes those marked close-on-exec (kern_descrip.c lines 2862-2889).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.39 – The child's JFT: duplicate each inheritable handle, 0FFh otherwise (MISC.ASM lines 412-452)Source ↗
        XOR     BX,BX                   ; dup all jfns
        MOV     CX,FilPerProc           ; only 20 of them

Create_dup_jfn:
        PUSH    ES                      ; save new PDB
        invoke  SFFromHandle            ; get sf pointer
        MOV     AL,-1                   ; unassigned JFN
        JC      CreateStash             ; file was not really open
        TEST    ES:[DI].sf_flags,sf_no_inherit
        JNZ     CreateStash             ; if no-inherit bit is set, skip dup.
⋮
        MOV     AH,BYTE PTR ES:[DI].sf_mode
        AND     AH,sharing_mask
        CMP     AH,sharing_net_fcb
        jz      CreateStash
⋮
        MOV     WORD PTR [THISSFT],DI
        MOV     WORD PTR [THISSFT+2],ES
        invoke  DOS_DUP                 ; signal duplication
⋮
        invoke  pJFNFromHandle          ; ES:DI is jfn
        MOV     AL,ES:[DI]              ; get sfn
;
; Take AL (old sfn or -1) and stash it into the new position
;
CreateStash:
        POP     ES
        MOV     ES:[BX].PDB_JFN_Table,AL; copy into new place!
        INC     BX                      ; next jfn...
        LOOP    create_dup_jfn

        MOV     BX,CurrentPDB           ; get current process
        MOV     ES:[PDB_Parent_PID],BX  ; stash in child
        MOV     [CurrentPDB],ES

Return to the parent. On MS-DOS the parent is frozen inside its INT 21h call. When the child exits, reset_environment (Listing 2.40) frees the child's memory and handles unless it is a TSR, makes the parent current again, reloads the parent's stack from PDB_User_stack and returns through the INT 22h address, which EXEC had set to the parent's return address. On FreeBSD both processes run on; the parent calls wait4, and exit1 has left the status in the zombie's struct proc (Section 2.6).

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 2.40 – reset_environment: free the child (unless TSR), resume the parent on its own saved stack (CTRLC.ASM lines 667-734)Source ↗
        CMP     AX,BX
        JZ      reset_return            ; parentPDB = CurrentPDB
        CMP     BX,CX
        JNZ     reset_return            ; CurrentPDB <> ThisPDB
        PUSH    AX                      ; save parent
        CMP     BYTE PTR [exit_type],Exit_keep_process
        JZ      reset_to_parent         ; keeping this process
⋮
        invoke  arena_free_process
⋮
        invoke  DOS_ABORT

reset_to_parent:
        POP     [CurrentPDB]            ; set up process as parent
⋮
        MOV     DS,[CurrentPDB]
        ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        MOV     SS,WORD PTR DS:[PDB_user_stack+2]
        MOV     SP,WORD PTR DS:[PDB_user_stack]

        ASSUME  SS:NOTHING
        invoke  restore_world
        ASSUME  ES:NOTHING
        MOV     User_SP,AX
        POP     AX                      ; suck off CS:IP of interrupt...
        POP     AX
        POP     AX
        MOV     AX,0F202h               ; STI
        PUSH    AX
        PUSH    WORD PTR [EXITHOLD+2]
        PUSH    WORD PTR [EXITHOLD]
        MOV     AX,User_SP
        IRET                            ; Long return back to user terminate address

What to notice. The child's view of "inherited state" differs in instructive ways:

State MS-DOS 4.00 EXEC FreeBSD fork + execve
Memory new blocks; parent's memory untouched but readable and writable by the child copy-on-write copy at fork, replaced by the new image at exec
Open files JFT copied, SFT ref counts +1, except sf_no_inherit and network handles descriptor table copied (fdcopy), except close-on-fork; close-on-exec closed at exec
Environment copied into a new block, followed by the program name passed explicitly as envp, copied onto the new stack
Current directory per drive, in the global CDS (MSCONST.ASM line 74), so shared with the parent per process (pwd), copied at fork (kern_fork.c lines 469-475)
Ctrl-C / error handlers INT 22h-24h vectors saved in the child's PSP, restored at exit caught signals reset to default at exec (execsigs, kern_sig.c lines 1081-1114)
Exit status one global word, read once with 4Dh per child, collected with wait4
Parent during child suspended inside INT 21h runs concurrently

Discussion questions.

  1. A child program runs CD \TEMP and exits. What is the parent's current directory now, on MS-DOS and on FreeBSD? Point to the data structure that decides.
  2. Why does reset_environment skip freeing memory when exit_type is Exit_keep_process, and what does that imply for the INT 21h vector a TSR has hooked?
  3. posix_spawn and vfork exist on FreeBSD. Which of the costs of fork + execve do they avoid, and does MS-DOS EXEC pay any of them?

Homework#

Hand in sources, transcripts and answers as one archive. Cite the source lines (permalinks) that support every explanation, as these notes do.

Exercise 2.1: An MCB walker#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write MCBWALK.COM (nasm, org 100h) for the MS-DOS 4.00 lab image. It calls function 52h, reads arena_head at ES:[BX-2], and prints one line per arena block: MCB segment, signature, owner (with "free" for 0 and "system" for 8), size in paragraphs and bytes, and the eight name bytes when the block is a program's PSP block. It stops after 'Z' and prints arena trashed if it meets any other signature, as check_signature would.

  • Run it from COMMAND.COM, from a second COMMAND started inside the first, and after loading a resident program of your choice. Explain every block in the three outputs.
  • Which block holds MCBWALK itself, and which its environment? Why is MCBWALK's own block so large (see step 4 of EXEC in Section 2.6), and what must a .COM program do before it can EXEC a child?

Hints: Listing 2.21, MSCONST.ASM lines 63-69, ALLOC.ASM lines 86-115. Print with function 09h ($-terminated strings) or 02h. Copy the program into the image as described in Module 0.

Template 2.1 – Skeleton of the walker (fill in the gaps)
        org     100h
        mov     ah, 52h
        int     21h                     ; ES:BX -> SYSINITVAR
        mov     ax, [es:bx-2]           ; arena_head: first MCB segment
next:   mov     es, ax
        ; print ES, ES:[0] (signature), ES:[1] (owner), ES:[3] (size), ES:[8..15] (name)
        ; if ES:[0] is not 'M' or 'Z': print "arena trashed" and exit
        ; if ES:[0] == 'Z': exit
        mov     ax, es
        add     ax, [es:3]
        inc     ax                      ; next = this + size + 1
        jmp     next

Exercise 2.2: A FAT12 reader in Python#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 4 h.

Write fat12.py that opens the lab floppy image read-only and:

  1. parses the BPB at offset 0Bh of sector 0 (layout: BOOTFORM.INC lines 10-36);
  2. computes the number of clusters and decides FAT12 or FAT16 with the rule of Section 2.4;
  3. lists the root directory (DIRENT.INC lines 28-40);
  4. for a file name given on the command line, prints its cluster chain and writes its contents to standard output.

Implement fat_entry(n) exactly as MAPCLUSTER + UNPACK do, and add a comment that cites the matching lines of FAT.ASM and of fatentry in msdosfs_fat.c. Test it on a cluster whose entry straddles two FAT sectors (Study case 2.B, question 1). Compare your output with TYPE under MS-DOS and with cat on the msdosfs mount of Exercise 2.3 (cmp the files).

Hints: use struct.unpack_from('<H', fat, n * 3 // 2). The root directory starts after the reserved sectors and all FAT copies; the data area after the root directory.

Exercise 2.3: Tracing a read on msdosfs#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

In the FreeBSD VM, copy the lab floppy image (Module 0, section 0.6), attach it with mdconfig -a -t vnode -f /tmp/dos400.img, and mount it read-only with mount_msdosfs -o ro /dev/mdN /mnt (use the unit mdconfig printed).

  1. Run truss cat /mnt/CONFIG.SYS (or any text file on the image). For each system call in the output, give its number and handler from syscalls.master, and say which hops of Study case 2.A it exercises.
  2. Run ktrace -t cnf cat /mnt/CONFIG.SYS and kdump. Which kdump lines come from the ktrsyscall call in subr_syscall.c lines 81-84, and which record type shows page faults (see vm_fault.c lines 749-752)?
  3. Optional: kldload dtraceall and count stacks with dtrace -n 'fbt::pcbmap:entry { @[stack()] = count(); }' while you cat a large file twice. Explain why the second run calls pcbmap less often. If the probe does not exist on your kernel, say so and use fbt::msdosfs_read:entry instead.

Deliverables: the transcripts, annotated.

Exercise 2.4: A system call of your own#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 4 h.

Start from the example module in /usr/src/share/examples/kld/syscall (syscall.c lines 37-83) and its test program (call.c lines 38-51). Build it with make, load it with kldload ./syscall.ko, and run the test.

  1. Change the system call to take one int argument and return twice its value in td->td_retval[0]; return EINVAL for a negative argument.
  2. Write a test that calls it with 21 and with -1 using syscall(2), and prints the return value and errno. Run it under truss.
  3. Explain, citing Listing 2.13 and Listing 2.10, how EINVAL becomes -1 with errno = 22 in your program. Which register and which flag carry the error between kernel and libc?
  4. Explain sy_narg and why the argument structure in sys/sys/sysproto.h pads every field (struct read_args, sysproto.h lines 42-46, and the PADL_/PADR_ macros above it).

Exercise 2.5: A TSR that counts INT 21h calls#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 5 h.

Write CNT21.COM, a TSR that hooks INT 21h, increments a 16-bit counter indexed by AH (256 entries), and chains to the previous handler with a far JMP (not CALL). It saves the old vector with function 35h, installs itself with 25h, and stays resident with 31h, keeping only the resident part. Provide a way for a second program, SHOW21.COM, to find the table (for example an otherwise unused vector that points at it) and print the non-zero counters.

Answer, citing listings:

  1. Why must the hook not print anything with INT 21h itself? Describe exactly what would be overwritten if it did, using Listing 2.3 and Listing 2.4.
  2. Why chain with JMP FAR rather than CALL FAR followed by IRET? Consider how SYS_RET_ERR returns the carry flag (Listing 2.6).
  3. Functions 4Bh, 4Ch and 31h do not return to the instruction after INT 21h in the usual way. Does your counter still count them? Why?
  4. Run SHOW21 after DIR. Which functions does COMMAND.COM use most?
Template 2.2 – Shape of the resident handler (not complete)
handler:
        push    bx
        mov     bl, ah
        xor     bh, bh
        shl     bx, 1
        inc     word [cs:counts+bx]     ; DS is the caller's; use CS:
        pop     bx
        jmp     far [cs:old21]          ; flags and registers untouched
old21   dd      0
counts  times 256 dw 0

Exercise 2.6: DUP, FORCEDUP and dup2, predicted then verified#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 1.5 h.

  1. A program opens A:\T.TXT and gets handle h, calls DUP on h, then FORCEDUP h onto 1, writes 10 bytes to handle 1, and calls LSEEK on h with offset 0 from the current position. Draw the JFT and the SFT entry (sf_ref_count, sf_position) after every call, and give h, the handle returned by DUP, and the value returned by LSEEK.
  2. Repeat in C on FreeBSD: fd = open(...), dup(fd), dup2(fd, 1), write(1, buf, 10), lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR), and check the reference count and offset with procstat -f (from a second shell, while the program sleeps before exiting).
  3. Trace FORCEDUP with BX = CX (a handle onto itself) through HANDLE.ASM lines 739-747, HANDLE.ASM lines 709-727 and CheckOwner (HANDLE.ASM lines 766-778). What does MS-DOS 4.00 return? What does FreeBSD's dup2(fd, fd) return (kern_descrip.c lines 1079-1084)?

Exercise 2.7: Essay: protection versus compatibility#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 2 h.

In 1,200-1,500 words, argue for or against this statement: "MS-DOS could not have added memory protection without breaking the programs that made it successful." Use at least four concrete mechanisms from this module (for example writable interrupt vectors, the InDOS flag, MCBs in user memory, BADCALL not setting carry, the error mapping table, the swappable data area) and contrast each with how FreeBSD 15.1 handles the same need. Cite source lines. Discuss what an 8088 with 256-640 KB of RAM made possible, and what later processors changed.
